# Bayesian inference and MCMC

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## From point estimates to posterior distributions

### Point estimation: least squares and maximum likelihood

- One [best]{style="color: tomato;"} value for each parameter, [$\hat{\theta}$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
- Uncertainty came afterwards, from [standard errors]{style="color: tomato;"} or the [profile likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The Bayesian formulation

So far we have asked *which* [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} fits best.

A Bayesian asks

["How plausible is each value of $\theta$, given the data?"]{style="color: tomato;"}

- The answer is a [probability distribution]{style="color: tomato;"} over [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
- Every estimate, interval and prediction we report comes from that one distribution

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bayesian inference is reallocation of credibility {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Before we see any data, each possible value of [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} has some [prior]{style="color: tomato;"} credibility
- The data then make some values more believable and others less
- [Bayes' rule]{style="color: tomato;"} is the rule for moving credibility towards the values that explain the data well
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
![](figures/06_bayes_update.png)
:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bayes' rule

::: {style="color: steelblue;"}
$$p(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}{p(y)}$$
:::

- [$p(\theta)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is the [prior]{style="color: tomato;"}, what we believed before seeing the data $y$
- [$p(y \mid \theta)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is the [likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}, the same function we maximised in the MLE section
- [$p(\theta \mid y)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is the [posterior]{style="color: tomato;"}, what we believe now
- [$p(y)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is a [normalising constant]{style="color: tomato;"}. It is the same number for every [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, so it does not change the shape of the posterior

::: {style="color: steelblue;"}
$$\text{posterior} \propto \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior}$$
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The prior

### Sources of prior information

- [Earlier outbreaks and the literature]{style="color: tomato;"}, for example the infectious period of influenza
- [Constraints]{style="color: tomato;"}: rates are positive, proportions lie between 0 and 1
- [Expert judgement]{style="color: tomato;"}: what the people who know the disease think

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Types of priors: vague and informative priors

- A [vague]{style="color: tomato;"} prior spreads credibility widely and leaves the work to the data
- An [informative]{style="color: tomato;"} prior writes down what we already know. It matters most when the data are thin
- Either way the prior is part of the model, so [say what it is, and check what it implies]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Prior predictive checks

:::::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Nobody has intuition for a prior on [$\beta$]{style="color: steelblue;"}. Everybody has intuition for an epidemic curve
- So [draw parameter values from the prior, run the model]{style="color: tomato;"}, and look at the epidemics it produces
- If half of them put the whole school in bed by day two, the prior is telling you something you did not intend
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
![](figures/06_flu_prior_predictive.png)
:::
:::::
::::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## {background-color="#447099" transition="fade-in"}

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
### Discussion

- What prior would you put on the infectious period of influenza? Of Ebola? Where would you get it from?
- Is a prior that puts the whole school in bed by day two "wrong", or just vague?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The posterior

### Posterior summaries: point estimates

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="38%"}
- If you want a single number, the posterior gives you three to choose from: the [mode]{style="color: tomato;"}, the [median]{style="color: tomato;"} and the [mean]{style="color: tomato;"}
- They agree when the posterior is symmetric and differ when it is skewed, as it usually is for a rate
- The [median is the usual choice]{style="color:tomato"}: it does not move when the tail is long
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](figures/06_posterior_point.png)
:::
:::::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Posterior summaries: credible intervals

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="38%"}
- A [95% credible interval]{style="color: tomato;"} is the range holding 95% of the posterior probability, here the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles
- You can read it literally: ["there is a 95% probability that $R_0$]{style="color: tomato;"} lies between [1.5 and 4.1]{style="color: steelblue;"}"
- A confidence interval is rather a statement about repeated sampling, not about [$R_0$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](figures/06_posterior_interval.png)
:::
:::::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Posterior summaries: derived quantities

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="38%"}
- We sample [$\beta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} and [$\gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, but what we want is [$R_0 = \beta N / \gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
- Compute it for every draw and you have its posterior, [correlation between the parameters]{style="color:tomato"} included, at no extra cost
- The same goes for the infectious period, the peak size, or the final attack rate
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](figures/06_posterior_derived.png)
:::
:::::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Posterior summaries: predictions

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="38%"}
- Run the model [once for each draw]{style="color:tomato"} and you get a whole [family of epidemic curves]{style="color:tomato"} rather than one
- Their spread is the [prediction uncertainty]{style="color: tomato;"} that comes from not knowing the parameters exactly
- [Summarise them]{style="color:tomato"} as a median curve and a 95% band, and compare the band with the data
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](figures/06_posterior_predictive.png)
:::
:::::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The posterior is intractable

### The normalising constant

::: {style="color: steelblue;"}
$$p(y) = \int p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)\, d\theta$$
:::

- This is an [integral over every combination of parameter values]{style="color: tomato;"}, and for an ODE model there is [no formula for it]{style="color:tomato"}.
- What we *can* do is evaluate [$p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} at any [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} we like, which gives us the posterior [up to that unknown constant]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The obvious approach: evaluate the posterior on a grid

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="38%"}
- We cannot integrate the posterior, but we can [evaluate it anywhere]{style="color: tomato;"}
- So choose a set of values for [$\beta$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, run the model at each, and record [$p(y \mid \beta)\, p(\beta)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
- With [$\gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"} held fixed, 15 values means [15 model runs]{style="color: tomato;"}, and the shape of the posterior appears
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](figures/06_grid_1d.png)
:::
:::::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Two parameters: a grid of grids

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="38%"}
- Now let [$\gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"} vary too: 15 values of each, so every value of [$\beta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is paired with every value of [$\gamma$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
- That is [$15 \times 15 = 225$]{style="color: steelblue;"} combinations, and [225 model runs]{style="color: tomato;"}
- A third parameter would multiply that by 15 again: a cube of [3,375]{style="color: steelblue;"} points
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](figures/06_grid_2d.png)
:::
:::::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Every extra parameter multiplies the cost by 15

```{.default include="results/06_grid_cost.txt" code-line-numbers="false"}
```

- The number of runs is [$15^p$]{style="color: steelblue;"} for [$p$]{style="color: steelblue;"} parameters: this is the [curse of dimensionality]{style="color: tomato;"}
- With two parameters a grid is a fine way to *look at* the posterior; an SEIR model with reporting and a latent period has six or more, and is [out of the question]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Grid evaluation for the influenza outbreak

![](figures/06_flu_grid_posterior.png)

- Worse, a grid spends its runs evenly, and the posterior is not spread evenly: over the range of the prior, [3,600]{style="color: steelblue;"} runs and [nearly all of them landed where the posterior is zero]{style="color: tomato;"}
- What we want is a method that spends its model runs [where the posterior is large]{style="color: tomato;"}, and that is what MCMC does

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Monte Carlo estimation {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
- If you want the mean height of the people of Kumasi you do not measure everyone. You measure a [sample]{style="color: tomato;"}
- A posterior can be treated the same way. Given enough draws of [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, the [mean, the quantiles and the histogram of the sample]{style="color: tomato;"} are as good as the real thing
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
![](figures/06_monte_carlo.png)
:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Two things you can do with a distribution

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
| | [Evaluate]{style="color: tomato;"} it at a point | [Sample]{style="color: tomato;"} from it |
|---|---|---|
| [$N(5, 2)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} | `dnorm(6, 5, 2)` gives 0.176 | `rnorm(3, 5, 2)` gives 6.3, 4.1, 7.8 |
| The posterior | `log_posterior(theta)`: one model run | there is no `rposterior()` |

- R provides both for the familiar distributions, so we never notice they are different abilities
- For the posterior we have only the first: any [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} can be scored, up to the constant [$p(y)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
- No function returns random draws from *this* posterior: it has no formula, it is whatever shape the model, the likelihood and the prior produce together
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Sampling from an unnormalised density

- Monte Carlo needs [samples]{style="color: tomato;"}: a bag of draws of [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} from which means, intervals and predictions are read off
- All we have is the ability to [evaluate]{style="color: tomato;"}: to score any candidate [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} and say how plausible it is relative to any other

[**How do you draw samples from something you can only evaluate?**]{style="color: tomato;"}

The answer is to stop trying to draw independent samples at all, and instead to walk through parameter space one step at a time, deciding each step from the scores of two candidates. The rest of this section is that walk

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Markov chain Monte Carlo {.smaller}

[**Core idea:**]{style="color: tomato;"} generate the samples one after another as a [chain]{style="color: tomato;"}, where each new value depends only on the one before it (that is what *Markov* means), and set up the rule for the next step so that the chain spends time in each region in proportion to the posterior density

- Start somewhere. Propose a small move. Accept or reject it depending on how the posterior changes. Repeat
- Run it long enough and the values in the chain are draws from the posterior, and we [never had to compute $p(y)$]{style="color: tomato;"}
- The original version is the [Metropolis algorithm]{style="color: tomato;"}, which is what we build next

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Metropolis algorithm {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
1.  Start at some [$\theta^{(0)}$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
2.  Propose [$\theta^* = \theta + \varepsilon$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, where [$\varepsilon$]{style="color: steelblue;"} comes from a [symmetric]{style="color: tomato;"} proposal distribution such as [$N(0, \sigma^2)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
3.  Compute [$r = \dfrac{p(\theta^* \mid y)}{p(\theta \mid y)}$]{style="color: steelblue;"}. The constant [$p(y)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} appears top and bottom and [cancels]{style="color: tomato;"}
4.  Draw [$u \sim U(0, 1)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}. If [$u < r$]{style="color: steelblue;"} [accept]{style="color: tomato;"} the move ([$\theta \leftarrow \theta^*$]{style="color: steelblue;"}); otherwise [stay where you are]{style="color: tomato;"}
5.  Record [$\theta$]{style="color: steelblue;"} and go back to step 2
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](figures/06_metropolis_flowchart.png)
:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The acceptance rule

![](figures/06_metropolis_step.png)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Consequences of the acceptance rule

- If the proposal has higher posterior density than where we are, we [always]{style="color: tomato;"} take it
- If it has lower density we take it [with probability $r$]{style="color: tomato;"}. The chain can walk downhill, which is why it explores the distribution instead of climbing to the top and staying there
- When a proposal is rejected the current value is [written down again]{style="color: tomato;"}. Those repeats are part of the sample, so do not throw them away
- Put together, the chain visits each region [in proportion to its posterior density]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Detailed balance and the stationary distribution

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- The acceptance rule gives the chain [detailed balance]{style="color: tomato;"}: as much probability flows from $\theta$ to $\theta^*$ as flows back, so nothing piles up anywhere [$$p(\theta \mid y)\, q(\theta^* \mid \theta)\, \alpha(\theta, \theta^*) = p(\theta^* \mid y)\, q(\theta \mid \theta^*)\, \alpha(\theta^*, \theta)$$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
- [$\alpha = \min(1, r)$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is the smallest correction that makes this hold
- The posterior is then the chain's [stationary distribution]{style="color: tomato;"}. Run it long enough and its values are posterior draws
- With an asymmetric proposal the ratio needs a correction. That is [Metropolis–Hastings]{style="color: tomato;"}: [$$r = \frac{p(\theta^* \mid y)\, q(\theta \mid \theta^*)}{p(\theta \mid y)\, q(\theta^* \mid \theta)}$$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

``` {.r include="scripts/06_mcmc_schematics.R" snippet="metropolis_1d" code-line-numbers="1-5|7-9|10-16|17-18|20"}
```

Everything is done on the [log scale]{style="color: tomato;"}, so the products become sums and the tiny likelihoods do not underflow to zero

The sampler knows nothing about Bayes. It will sample from anything you can evaluate, so try it first on [$N(5, 2)$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, where we know what the answer should look like.

``` {.r include="scripts/06_mcmc_schematics.R" snippet="metropolis_normal"}
```

## Practical implementation

### Tuning the proposal

![](figures/06_proposal_tuning.png)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Proposal scale and acceptance rate

- Make the proposal [too narrow]{style="color: tomato;"} and nearly every move is accepted, but each move is tiny and the chain crawls
- Make it [too wide]{style="color: tomato;"} and nearly every move is rejected, so the chain sits still for long stretches
- For a random walk proposal, aim for an acceptance rate of about [44% with one parameter, down to about 23% with many]{style="color: tomato;"}
- If the parameters are [correlated]{style="color: tomato;"} in the posterior, the proposal should be correlated the same way

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Burn-in

![](figures/06_burn_in.png)

- We chose the starting point, so the first part of the chain says more about that choice than about the posterior
- Throw those early samples away. This is the [burn-in]{style="color: tomato;"}. Discarding a few extra costs little, and starting from a sensible place such as the MLE shortens it
- How much to discard is decided [after looking at the chain]{style="color: tomato;"}, never before

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Convergence assessment with multiple chains

![](figures/06_convergence.png)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Convergence diagnostics

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
- A single chain cannot tell you about the places it has never been
- So start [several chains far apart]{style="color: tomato;"}. If they end up indistinguishable, they have found the same distribution
- [$\hat{R}$]{style="color: tomato;"} turns that into a number by comparing the variance between chains with the variance within them. We want [$\hat{R}$ below 1.01]{style="color: steelblue;"}
- Consecutive draws are correlated, so 20,000 of them carry less information than 20,000 independent draws would. The [effective sample size]{style="color: tomato;"} is the number that matters

``` {.r include="scripts/06_mcmc_schematics.R" snippet="rhat"}
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Convergence checklist

- The [trace plots]{style="color: tomato;"} show no trend, the same spread at the start as at the end, and the chains lie on top of each other
- The [acceptance rate]{style="color: tomato;"} is in a sensible range
- [$\hat{R}$]{style="color: steelblue;"} is close to 1 and the [effective sample size]{style="color: tomato;"} is in the hundreds at least
- [Any of these checks can show you a problem. None of them can prove there is not one]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Beyond the Metropolis algorithm {.smaller}

- [Metropolis-within-Gibbs]{style="color: tomato;"} updates one parameter, or one block of parameters, at a time, which helps when the parameters are correlated
- [Adaptive MCMC]{style="color: tomato;"} learns the proposal covariance from the chain while it runs, so you do not have to tune it by hand
- [Hamiltonian Monte Carlo]{style="color: tomato;"}, and its self-tuning version NUTS, uses the gradient of the log posterior to propose long moves in a sensible direction. It is the default sampler in Stan
- [Particle MCMC]{style="color: tomato;"} is for stochastic models, where the likelihood itself has to be estimated by simulation. That is the next section

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Probabilistic programming languages

- You write down the [model, the prior and the likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}. The software does the sampling and reports the diagnostics
- Stan (through `rstan` or `cmdstanr`), `nimble`, `brms`, PyMC and Turing.jl all work this way

## The Bayesian workflow

1.  Write down the [model and the prior]{style="color: tomato;"}, and check the prior by simulating from it
2.  Write down the [likelihood]{style="color: tomato;"}, that is, how the data arise from the model
3.  [Sample the posterior]{style="color: tomato;"} with MCMC, using several chains started far apart
4.  [Check the chains]{style="color: tomato;"}: trace plots, acceptance rate, [$\hat{R}$]{style="color: steelblue;"}, effective sample size
5.  [Summarise the posterior]{style="color: tomato;"}: means, credible intervals, and derived quantities such as [$R_0$]{style="color: steelblue;"}
6.  [Check the fit]{style="color: tomato;"} by plotting posterior predictions against the data

------------------------------------------------------------------------
